question.:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $xy+{x}^{2}=1.$ The normal line at the point $(1,\,0)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(1,\,0).$   Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{x}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2x & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-(2x+y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,0)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2x+y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 1+0}{1} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $$
\displaystyle {m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(1,\,0)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-0) & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(0-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,-\frac{1}{2}).$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(4,4).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{'},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}8y & ={x}^{2}+4x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+4x) \\ 8\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+4 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+4}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+2}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{x+2}{4}\right)|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{4+2}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

We can write the equation of the normal line at the point $(4,4)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{'}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-4) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{8}{3} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{20}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P,$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{20}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}x & =\frac{20}{3} \\ x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(10,\,0).$

question.:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}=8.$ The tangent line at the point $(1,\,1)$ on the curve intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\,1).$  

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 4x+12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-4x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{12y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{x}{3y}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-1) & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(0-1)+1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,\frac{4}{3}).$

question.:question/problem: The equation of a curve is ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$ The normal line at the point $(-3,\,1)$ on the curve intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(-3,\,1).$  Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x-6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x}{-6y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(-3,\,1)$ is 

 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{x}{3y}\right)}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is ${m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-1}=1.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(-3,\,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-1) & =1(x+3) \\ y & =(x+3)+1 \\ y & =x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+4 \\ 0 & =x+4 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-4,\,0).$

The equation of a curve is ${x}^{2}+xy=6{y}^{2}.$ The normal line at the point $(2,1)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

The coordinates of $P$ are $($

{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(2,1).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy & =6{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ 2x+(y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ 2x+y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ (x-12y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}\right)|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-2(2)-1}{2-12(1)} \\  & =\frac{(-5)}{(-10)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=-2.
$$

We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(2,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-2(x-2) \\ y-1 & =-2x+4 \\ y & =-2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+5 \\ y & =-2(0)+5 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,5).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(36) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(36) \\ 8x+18y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 18y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-8x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{8x}{18y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{9y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(0,2)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(0,\,2)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{4x}{9y}\right)|}_{(0,\,2)} \\  & =-\frac{4\cdot 0}{9\cdot 2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =0(x-0) \\ y & =2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) \\ 8x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =20 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =20-8x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{20-8x}{2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{10-4x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{10-4x}{y}\right)|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{10-4\cdot 4}{4} \\  & =\frac{(-6)}{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{3}{2}(x-4) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}(x-4)+4 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}x+10\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{3}{2}x+10 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot 0+10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}

The equation $xy=5$ represents a hyperbola. The tangent line at the point $(1,5)$ on the hyperbola intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,5).$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5) \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-y}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,5)$  is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,5)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,5)} \\  & =-\frac{5}{1} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(1,\,5)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-5) & =-5(x-1) \\ y & =-5(x-1)+5 \\ y & =-5x+10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-5x+10 \\ y & =-5\cdot 0+10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,10).$
